title: Node 24 compatibility
need_summary: How to fix the Node 24 breakage caused by the removal of SlowBuffer in the crypto timing‑safe equality code, resolved by upgrading the transitive `jwa` dependency (e.g., to 1.4.2/2.0.1) as documented in PR #1007 and the jsonwebtoken 9.0.3 release.
security_topic: transitive-dependency compatibility with Node 24
question_text: Node 24 is approaching the LTS release. Can we upgrade or will the library be incompatible with Node 24?
answer_text:
We've released [patched versions](https://github.com/auth0/node-jwa/releases) of the `jwa` transitive dependency. These releases take care of not using the deprecated code when `crypto.timingSafeEqual()` is available (while still using it when run in legacy codebase with EOL Node.js versions where it wasn't available).

Running `npm upgrade jwa` (or whichever package manager alternative you happen to use) will pick those patched versions up and fix the issue for you.

I will leave this issue open to hopefully avoid new issues from being open and will comment again when a Node.js release with the [deprecated (but not removed)](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/58211) functionality is available.

Edit: [Node.js v24.0.1](https://github.com/nodejs/node/releases/tag/v24.0.1) was released on 2025-05-08 which reverts the problematic removal, it will still be removed in v25.x in October, but with the release of jwa@1.4.2 and jwa@2.0.1 these APIs are no longer in use so long as you upgrade your dependency tree, e.g. via `npm upgrade jwa`.

ISSUE #992: Node 24 compatibility
Author: benfosterlitmos
Date: 2025-05-07T01:12:40Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
### Description

`jsonwebtoken` doesn't work with Node 24. The `buffer-equal-constant-time` library  throws an error:

Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'prototype')

at

var origSlowBufEqual = SlowBuffer.prototype.equal;

buffer-equal-constant-time is a nested dep: `jsonwebtoken > jws > jwa > buffer-equal-constant-time`

### Reproduction

Initialize a new Node project and install jsonwebtoken.

Run the following JS using Node 24.0.0

```js
import jsonwebtoken from "jsonwebtoken";

jsonwebtoken.sign({ text: "test" }, "ABC");
```

Result:
```bash
var origSlowBufEqual = SlowBuffer.prototype.equal;
                                  ^

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'prototype')
    at Object.<anonymous> (/Users/user/testnode24/node_modules/buffer-equal-constant-time/index.js:37:35)
    at Module._compile (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1734:14)
    at Object..js (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1899:10)
    at Module.load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1469:32)
    at Module._load (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1286:12)
    at TracingChannel.traceSync (node:diagnostics_channel:322:14)
    at wrapModuleLoad (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:235:24)
    at Module.require (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1491:12)
    at require (node:internal/modules/helpers:135:16)
    at Object.<anonymous> (/Users/user/testnode24/node_modules/jwa/index.js:1:19)

Node.js v24.0.0
```

### Environment

- jsonwebtoken 9.0.2
- Node 24.0.0
- MacOS Sequoia

Running in Node 22 works without any issues.

[c1] @panva 2025-05-07T06:30:13Z:
Both runtime-deprecation and EOL of said Node.js API happened in the same major, that shouldn't have happened. https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/58211
---
[c2] @panva 2025-05-07T10:41:16Z:
I've tagged https://github.com/auth0/node-jwa/pull/52 internally to work around the deprecation and unintended removal (that https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/58211 will also resolve)
---
[c3] @panva 2025-05-07T12:13:06Z:
We've released [patched versions](https://github.com/auth0/node-jwa/releases) of the `jwa` transitive dependency. These releases take care of not using the deprecated code when `crypto.timingSafeEqual()` is available (while still using it when run in legacy codebase with EOL Node.js versions where it wasn't available).

Running `npm upgrade jwa` (or whichever package manager alternative you happen to use) will pick those patched versions up and fix the issue for you.

I will leave this issue open to hopefully avoid new issues from being open and will comment again when a Node.js release with the [deprecated (but not removed)](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/58211) functionality is available.

Edit: [Node.js v24.0.1](https://github.com/nodejs/node/releases/tag/v24.0.1) was released on 2025-05-08 which reverts the problematic removal, it will still be removed in v25.x in October, but with the release of jwa@1.4.2 and jwa@2.0.1 these APIs are no longer in use so long as you upgrade your dependency tree, e.g. via `npm upgrade jwa`.
---
[c4] @mvantellingen 2025-05-07T20:36:44Z:
Nice to see how quickly this is resolved, however I don't think it's possible to update the jwa dependency. It seems that `jsonwebtoken@9.0.2` has a dependency on jws `^3.2.2`, which depends on jwa `^1.4.1`. So it doesn't seem possible to update jwa to the latest version (2.0.1).

[c5] @panva 2025-05-08T05:49:11Z:
> Nice to see how quickly this is resolved, however I don't think it's possible to update the jwa dependency. It seems that `jsonwebtoken@9.0.2` has a dependency on jws `^3.2.2`, which depends on jwa `^1.4.1`. So it doesn't seem possible to update jwa to the latest version (2.0.1).

We did a release for both 1.x and 2.x major version release lines of jwa. They're both visible on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/jwa?activeTab=versions) and [github](https://github.com/auth0/node-jwa/releases) and v1.4.2 does get picked up during dependency tree upgrades since it is within the declared semver range.

Yes **v25 rc.1** is failing because of that issue.

I don't understand if the update to node 24 will work automatically or if I'll need to change something.

[c11] @Maxou44 2025-10-20T19:03:24Z:
Node.js 25 has been released, and I encountered the same issue with the "slim" Docker image. Switching the image to "lts-slim" resolved the problem.
---
[c12] @dpecos 2025-10-28T10:14:24Z:
Wouldn't it be easier to just release a new version of both the `jws` (using the correct `jwa` version) and `jsonwebtoken` (using the fixed `jws` version) rather than forcing consumers to fix those transient dependencies?

This is major issue happening to anyone using Node 25, and expecting everyone to land in this issue thread to solve the issue does not sound like a proper way of dealing with it.

Just my 2 cents.
---
[c13] @ShahandFahad 2025-10-29T05:40:11Z:
I just updated to Node.js `v25.0.0` and encountered the exact same error.  Running `npm upgrade jwa` resolved the issue for me.
---
[c14] @pavelbabenko 2025-11-07T10:30:00Z:
For those who use `yarn` - add this to you `package.json`
```
"resolutions": {
    "jwa": "^2.0.1"
 },
```
---
[c15] @kvz 2025-12-01T14:04:36Z:
Seeing the same failure on Node 25 (SlowBuffer removed). Stack: buffer-equal-constant-time -> jwa -> jws -> jsonwebtoken (pulled in via @slack/bolt). Quick workaround: patch buffer-equal-constant-time to fall back to Buffer when SlowBuffer is undefined (and optionally shim Buffer.prototype.equal = Buffer.prototype.equals). Production on Node 24 is fine; local dev on 25 explodes before our code runs. It would be great to ship a fix in a patch release or upstream to buffer-equal-constant-time.
---
[c16] @mbtools 2025-12-12T17:44:55Z:
Closed by https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/pull/1007 which is in [9.0.3](https://www.npmjs.com/package/jsonwebtoken)

@mbtools , just checking in: Did you forget to close this issue? Does `node-jsonwebtoken` support Node 24?
---
[c18] @mbtools 2026-03-13T12:19:50Z:
I'm not a maintainer and was just connecting the dots. But someone with permissions should close it 😁

title: Node.js 'crypto' module error in jsonwebtoken
need_summary: The developer needed to know that the edge runtime lacks Node.js 'crypto', preventing jsonwebtoken from working, and the concrete workaround is to switch to the 'jose' package (see https://www.npmjs.com/package/jose) or refer to Vercel’s edge runtime documentation (https://vercel.com/docs/functions/runtimes/edge#edge-runtime-supported-apis).
security_topic: edge runtime incompatibility with Node.js crypto module for JWT
question_text:
Recently, I have used jwt in nextjs but the nextjs gives me error below
[Error: The edge runtime does not support Node.js 'crypto' module.
I hope the problem will be solved very soon. Thank you
answer_text:
Same issue when you use this on cloudflare workers.
switched to https://www.npmjs.com/package/jose takes care of that.

title: What happened? The performance of jsonwebtoken 9.0.2 is 50 times slower than 8.5.1
need_summary: The developer needed to know that the performance regression was caused by a security fix introduced in commit ecdf6cc6073ea13a7e71df5fad043550f08d0fa6, and the answer cites that commit as the concrete reference.
security_topic: performance regression caused by security-related KeyObject change
question_text: What happened? The performance of jsonwebtoken 9.0.2 is 50 times slower than 8.5.1
answer_text:
Confirmed the performance regression. Looks like it was introduced in https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/commit/ecdf6cc6073ea13a7e71df5fad043550f08d0fa6 by adding a `crypto.createSecretKey` call to create a `KeyObject` instead of using the string secret or PEM file. This was done to address some security vulnerabilities.

The regression can be workaround in 9.0.2 by passing a `KeyObject` directly to sign/verify methods.
thread_text:
ISSUE #966: What happened? The performance of jsonwebtoken 9.0.2 is 50 times slower than 8.5.1
Author: VxRain
Date: 2024-04-11T15:41:50Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]

### Description

The performance of jsonwebtoken 9.0.2 is 50 times slower than 8.5.1, mainly in the HS256 algorithm. 
**The encoding speed has slowed down by 53 times, and the decoding speed by 34 times.**


#### 8.5.1 benchmark results
Encoding
HS256 x 120,423 ops/sec ±0.33% (91 runs sampled)
RS256 x 793 ops/sec ±0.50% (94 runs sampled)
ES256 x 2,418 ops/sec ±0.99% (94 runs sampled)
Fastest encoder is HS256

Decoding
HS256 x 87,990 ops/sec ±0.93% (95 runs sampled)
RS256 x 5,921 ops/sec ±0.89% (93 runs sampled)
ES256 x 4,763 ops/sec ±0.77% (94 runs sampled)
Fastest decoder is HS256

---

#### 9.0.2 benchmark results
Encoding
HS256 x 2,264 ops/sec ±4.58% (78 runs sampled)
RS256 x 759 ops/sec ±0.73% (93 runs sampled)
ES256 x 2,131 ops/sec ±1.08% (91 runs sampled)
Fastest encoder is HS256

Decoding
HS256 x 2,568 ops/sec ±0.93% (93 runs sampled)
RS256 x 5,527 ops/sec ±1.60% (87 runs sampled)
ES256 x 3,871 ops/sec ±1.62% (91 runs sampled)
Fastest decoder is RS256



### Reproduction

[https://github.com/VxRain/node-jwt-benchmark](https://github.com/VxRain/node-jwt-benchmark)

### Environment

- **Node: v20.12.2**
- **System: Win11**
- **CPU: AMD R7 5800H**


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @panga 2024-04-15T20:56:22Z:
Confirmed the performance regression. 

Looks like it was introduced in https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/commit/ecdf6cc6073ea13a7e71df5fad043550f08d0fa6 by adding a `crypto.createSecretKey` call to create a `KeyObject` instead of using the string secret or PEM file. This was done to address some security vulnerabilities.

The regression can be workaround in 9.0.2 by passing a `KeyObject` directly to sign/verify methods.

title: Signature generation fails for SM2 private keys with ES256 algorithm for node 18 version
need_summary: The developer needed to know if SM2 private keys can be used with the ES256 algorithm in jsonwebtoken, and the maintainer confirmed they are unsupported for JOSE per the IANA algorithm registry and Node.js limitations (see IANA JOSE list and Node PR #37066).
security_topic: unsupported SM2 key usage with ES256 algorithm
question_text: `jwt.sign(<payload>, <utf8 encoded SM2 private key>, { algorithm: 'ES256' })` fails with "error":{"code":"ERR_OSSL_INVALID_DIGEST","library":"Provider routines","reason":"invalid digest"} when using node 18.17.0. The above command works fine with node version 16 but fails with node versions 18 and 20.
answer_text: There is no registered JWS algorithm for SM2 keys[^iana] and ES256 requires the use of an EC key using the P-256 curve. Furthermore Node.js does not fully support SM2 keys.[^node] Bottom line use of SM2 keys with JOSE is unsupported and out of scope.

The above command works fine with node version 16 but fails with node versions 18 and 20.

There is no registered JWS algorithm for SM2 keys[^iana] and ES256 requires the use of an EC key using the P-256 curve. Furthermore Node.js does not fully support SM2 keys.[^node]

Bottom line use of SM2 keys with JOSE is unsupported and out of scope.

[^iana]: https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml#web-signature-encryption-algorithms

security_topic: browser compatibility of server‑only JWT library
question_text: Importing `decode` function from jsonwebtoken causes error. I am unable to import the 'decode' function as normal.
answer_text: Yeah I had this, in my case it's caused by me trying to run it in the browser. See this https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/issues/931#issuecomment-1699100865. Run it on a node.js server - not a browser - and it's fine.

title: TypeError: Right hand side of instanceof is not an object
need_summary: The developer needed to know that jsonwebtoken 9.x fails on Bun because required crypto APIs are missing, and the concrete workaround is to downgrade to version 8.5.1 (or switch to panva/jose), as referenced in the comments with version numbers and a repository link.
security_topic: runtime incompatibility causing TypeError in jsonwebtoken on Bun
question_text:
When generating a token using the jsonwebtoken library instead of returning a valid token it returns an error:
```
108 |   if (secretOrPrivateKey != null && !(secretOrPrivateKey instanceof KeyObject)) {
                                         ^
TypeError: Right hand side of instanceof is not an object
```
Using valid code: `const token = await jwt.sign({ username: username }, jwtSecret);`
Returns a jwt token on versions prior to 9.0.0, preferably 8.5.1 works without issues.
answer_text:

title: Vulnerability / Unexpected Token Verification Behavior with Private Key
need_summary: The developer asked why JWT verification succeeds when using a private key and whether this is a security issue, and the maintainer answered that jsonwebtoken automatically derives the public key from the private key via Node.js's createPublicKey function (see the Node.js crypto documentation).
security_topic: private key usage for JWT verification
question_text: Token verification using the private key should fail, as the private key is meant for signing, not verification. However, token verification using the private key surprisingly succeeds, which contradicts the expected behavior. I would appreciate assistance in understanding if this is an issue or if there's a valid explanation for this behavior.
answer_text: This behavior should be better documented. This library simply uses createPublicKey which detects the key type and automatically derives the public key from private keys. I would not consider this to be a security issue since the key derivation only occurs when the key material is known to represent a private key.

[c0]
Issue Title: Unexpected Token Verification Behavior with Private Key

Description:
I've encountered unexpected behavior while using the jsonwebtoken library for token verification. As per best practices, I'm aware that token verification should use the public key, but I noticed that token verification is succeeding even when using the private key.

Steps to Reproduce:

Generate an RSA key pair using the crypto module.
Sign a JWT using the private key with the RS256 algorithm.
Attempt to verify the JWT using the private key instead of the public key.
Expected Behavior:
Token verification using the private key should fail, as the private key is meant for signing, not verification.

Actual Behavior:
Token verification using the private key surprisingly succeeds, which contradicts the expected behavior.

Environment:

Node.js version: v16.19.0
jsonwebtoken library version: 9.0.1/8.5.1 -> In these versions I have checked.
Operating System: Windows 10

Additional Information:
I've verified this behavior in multiple environments to ensure accuracy. It's important to clarify that this behavior goes against established best practices for token verification. I would appreciate assistance in understanding if this is an issue or if there's a valid explanation for this behavior.

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @ArielPrevu3D 2023-09-27T22:06:20Z:
This behavior should be better documented. This library simply uses [createPublicKey](https://nodejs.org/api/crypto.html#cryptocreatepublickeykey) which detects the key type and automatically derives the public key from private keys. 

I would not consider this to be a security issue since the key derivation only occurs when the key material is known to represent a private key.
---
[c2] @guda-art 2023-11-17T06:45:02Z:
Until now, I cannot understand the advantages of using private key signature and public key verification for the use of jwt
can  you tell me thanks !
@AbdullahSoomroOfficial 
---
[c3] @AbdullahSoomroOfficial 2023-11-17T12:26:06Z:
@guda-art
Public/Private key(Public key cryptography) is one of the way we can use to do two things:
1. To encrypt data
2. To create digital signature

For example In a web app if we use jwt for authentication.
In that case we do not want to encrypt any data.
But instead we want to sign a token(To create digital signature) to ensure data integrity and authenticity.
For that we first hash the data and sign it with our private key and issue it to client.
Later on the client side we can verify the token using our public key.
From verification we will get two surities:
1. Issuer of the token is the one who it says it is.
2. Data is tempered or not.

So by using public/private key we can securely transmit any data over http

title: secretOrPrivateKey size error when size is larger enough
need_summary: Developers needed to know that RS256 requires a minimum 2048‑bit key and can resolve the "secretOrPrivateKey has a minimum key size of 2048 bits" error by verifying key size, generating a proper key, switching to an ES algorithm, or enabling the allowInsecureKeySizes flag, as documented in RFC 7518.
security_topic: minimum RSA key size requirement for RS256 and how to resolve key size errors
question_text: I'm doing some development with octokit and probot which bring jsonwebtoken as a dependency. After updating octokit/auth-app to a version that supports jsonwebtoken 9.0.1, I'm getting this error: "secretOrPrivateKey has a minimum key size of 2048 bits for RS256". The private key used is definitely longer than 2048 bits, so I was not expecting to see this error.
answer_text:
For anyone stumbling over this issue:

First check the bit length of your key 

```
$ PRIVATE_KEY_FILE="private.pem"
$ openssl rsa -in $PRIVATE_KEY_FILE -text -noout | grep "Private-Key"
```

The reported bit length should be >= 2048. If your key has less then 2048 bits you have the following options:

1.) Gnerate a new key pair:

```
openssl genrsa -out private.pem 2048
openssl rsa -in private.pem -pubout -out public.pem
```

2.) Switch to one of the `ES*` algorithms

3.) If for some reasons you can not change your keys, you might set the flag `allowInsecureKeySizes` to true. 
Although this is not recommended as 1024 bit keys are considered weak nowadays. Also the RFC7518 requires at least 2048 bit keys.

> A key of size 2048 bits or larger MUST be used with these algorithms.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7518.html#section-3.3

@conioX ~33% of the keys generated by cryptotools.net are only 2047 bit long even if you asked for a 2048 bit long key. Cryptotools.net seems to use JSEncrypt to generate the keys. There is an [open issue](https://github.com/travist/jsencrypt/issues/33) regarding this topic over at JSEncrypt.

Fun fact about those 2047 bit keys is that node v16 reports 2048 bit for them whereas node v18 reports 2047bit. Probably the reason it fails in docker alpine (node:18.14-alpine3.17) and not on your windows machine.

comments.author: conioX
pixtron
comments.body:
For anyone stumbling over this issue:

First check the bit length of your key 

```
$ PRIVATE_KEY_FILE="private.pem"
$ openssl rsa -in $PRIVATE_KEY_FILE -text -noout | grep "Private-Key"
```

The reported bit length should be >= 2048. If your key has less then 2048 bits you have the following options:

1.) Gnerate a new key pair:

```
openssl genrsa -out private.pem 2048
openssl rsa -in private.pem -pubout -out public.pem
```

2.) Switch to one of the `ES*` algorithms

3.) If for some reasons you can not change your keys, you might set the flag `allowInsecureKeySizes` to true. 
Although this is not recommended as 1024 bit keys are considered weak nowadays. Also the RFC7518 requires at least 2048 bit keys.

> A key of size 2048 bits or larger MUST be used with these algorithms.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7518.html#section-3.3

@conioX ~33% of the keys generated by cryptotools.net are only 2047 bit long even if you asked for a 2048 bit long key. Cryptotools.net seems to use JSEncrypt to generate the keys. There is an [open issue](
https://github.com/travist/jsencrypt/issues/33) regarding this topic over at JSEncrypt.

Fun fact about those 2047 bit keys is that node v16 reports 2048 bit for them whereas node v18 reports 2047bit. Probably the reason it fails in docker alpine (node:18.14-alpine3.17) and not on your windows machine.

title: Crypto - KeyObject is undefined for Node V14 - "jsonwebtoken": "9.0.0"
need_summary: The developer needed to know why KeyObject is undefined when using jsonwebtoken on Node v14.10.1, and the answer cites the Node.js v14.10.1 crypto documentation confirming KeyObject exists only in the Node runtime (https://nodejs.org/docs/v14.10.1/api/crypto.html#crypto_class_keyobject).
security_topic: jsonwebtokens incompatibility with browser environment leading to undefined KeyObject
question_text: KeyObject from Crypto is undefined. I am using Node 14.10.1.
answer_text:
Indeed, `KeyObject` is present in Node.js v14.10.1. This library's use outside of Node.js runtime was never intended. Versions before 9.0.0 could use webpack's polyfill of the Node.js built-in modules. This most likely a) relied on slow js cryptography that isn't maintained anymore and lacks feature parity with Node's crypto and b) increased your js bundle size considerably. FWIW webpack 5 also no longer defaults to using these questionable crypto polyfills anymore.

It is better to rely on JWT modules made to be consumed in browser or generic javascript environments. You can discover such modules on jwt.io (https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript) under "JavaScript" libraries.

title: jsonwebtoken v9 verify function doesn't work in typescript

security_topic: incompatibility of jsonwebtoken v9 with React Native / browser environments

`jsonwebtoken` is a Node.js module, always was, its use in a browser or React-Native environments was never intended. It is better to rely on JWT modules made to be consumed in browser or generic javascript environments. You can discover such modules on https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript under "JavaScript" libraries.

ISSUE #877: Vulnerability in v8
Author: nirapx
Date: 2023-01-11T09:43:29Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
### Description

It seems that in v9 you fixed the vulnerability: `CVE-2022-23529` Arbitrary File Write via verify function.
I'm using `jsonwebtoken` v8 on Node v8 (legacy system) and I can't upgrade it.
Is there a patch for this vulnerability in v8?

### Environment

- **Version of this library used: 8**
- **Version of the platform or framework used, if applicable: Node 8**


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @aegilops 2023-01-11T20:45:17Z:
To trigger this "vulnerability" you would need to deserialize untrusted input and pass it straight to the `verify` function without validating it.

Not only that, you'd need to use a library that can deserialize functions as members of objects, which is very unusual, and it would need to preserve the case of the object property.

As long as you don't do that in your app, you cannot trigger this bug.

More details on [my LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/paul-h-579a1a243_jwt-cveabr2022abr23529-cve-activity-7018672384761081856-ar8S)

You do need to take more care with 8.5.1, since 9.0.0 is secure by design, but if you validate the inputs to `verify` and test your app then you can have some confidence - not every app built with 8.5.1 is automatically broken!

P.S. I work for GitHub, but not for the Advisory team and this is written in a personal capacity
---
[c2] @TinkCai 2023-01-12T05:31:06Z:
We're using a serverless service and the cloud provider only provides Nodejs8.9 and Nodejs10.15, so we can't upgrade it to a higher Nodejs version.
It's Nodejs10.15 with jsonwebtoken@9.0.0, when `jwt.sign` is called, an exception will happen.

errMsg: TypeError: Right-hand side of 'instanceof' is not an object
    at Object.module.exports [as sign] (:34560/var/user/node_modules/jsonwebtoken/sign.js:108)

I'm wondering if 9.x.x can support this case.
---
[c3] @Uzlopak 2023-01-12T06:02:05Z:
This is because KeyObject is added and exported in node version 11. 

You could theoretically use a library like proxyquire. So e.g. in your code you do 

```js
const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken')
```

Instead you do 

```js
const jwt = proxyquire('jsonwebtoken', { crypto: { KeyObject: Object } })
```

proxyquire will manipulate the  require call to crypto in jsonwebtoken and because we defined KeyObject as Object, it will return that. So the instanceof check will be not against undefined but Object.

This would also mean. that the proposed security vulnerability bugfix is basically patched out ;).

Check the performance. 
---
[c4] @arovetto 2023-01-13T07:46:42Z:
I agree with @nirapx, I also need the patch for CVE-2022-23529 on branch 8 without the breaking changes on v9.
Thanks
---
[c5] @aegilops 2023-01-13T17:34:38Z:
You don't *need* such a patch though, I don't think. I agree a point release would have been sensible, even though I think it's unlikely to be necessary.

The likelihood of an app deserializing a function and passing it straight to the secret used to validate JWT is tiny - it would be a huge design flaw and entirely break the authentication model of the app.

Most JSON libraries can't even deserialize a function, and the one that can needs a non-standard config to trigger the bug.

There may be other ways to deserialize data into objects that does this, yes, but it is still very unlikely that any app would accept untrusted data as secrets with no validation.
---
[c6] @BrianCraig 2023-01-16T09:17:22Z:
This vulnerability decision looks extremely arbitrary, if the parameter passed is supposedly from user input, how does it even gets evaluated? Almost every library would have the same "exploit".
This doesn't make any sense, not using eval on user input is a must in js development
---
[c7] @arovetto 2023-01-23T17:15:33Z:
I agree with you all. Applications consuming the library hardly are affected by the vulnerability. However, it's hard to explain and justify with stakeholders that the software is not affected when reports assert the opposite, and also my build pipeline perform a npm audit to check for any high and critical vulnerable libraries to be updated, that now it fails.
So unless the vulnerability will be de-classed, I would appreciate a lot if you could backport to patch also on v8.
Thanks

title: Regression between v8 and v9 when used in a Single Page Application (the library is run in a web browser)
need_summary: The developer asked if jsonwebtoken can be used safely in a browser and the maintainer clarified that it is Node‑only, browser polyfills (see crypto-browserify) are unmaintained and insecure, and recommends using browser‑compatible JWT libraries listed on jwt.io.
security_topic: incompatibility of node-jsonwebtoken with browser environments
question_text:
Using v9.0.0 in a SPA (the code is run in a web browser) doesn't work anymore, the last working version was v8.5.1

In the web browser console I get following error:
```
TypeError: invalid 'instanceof' operand KeyObject
    exports verify.js:120
    getSecret verify.js:97
    exports verify.js:101
```

When using the debugger it tells me that KeyObject is undefined:
```
 if (secretOrPublicKey != null && !(secretOrPublicKey instanceof KeyObject)) {
```

The culprit is following import that returns undefined objects: 
```
const {KeyObject, createSecretKey, createPublicKey} = require("crypto");
```

I tried to force the integration of "cryto" in my package.json, but it didn't change anything.

Thank you by advance for your help!
answer_text:
`jsonwebtoken` is a Node.js module, always was, its use in a browser was never intended. Versions before 9.0.0 could use webpack's polyfill of the Node.js built-in modules. This most likely a) relied on slow js cryptography that isn't [maintained anymore](https://www.npmjs.com/package/crypto-browserify) and lacks feature parity with Node's crypto and b) increased your js bundle size considerably. FWIW webpack 5 also no longer defaults to using these questionable crypto polyfills anymore.

It is better to rely on JWT modules made to be consumed in browser environments. You can discover such modules on [jwt.io](https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript) under "JavaScript" libraries.

  if (secretOrPrivateKey != null && !(secretOrPrivateKey instanceof KeyObject))

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
`jsonwebtoken` is a Node.js module, its use in a browser was never intended. Versions before 9.0.0 could use webpack's polyfill of the Node.js built-in modules. This most likely a) relied on slow js cryptography that isn't [maintained anymore](https://www.npmjs.com/package/crypto-browserify) and lacks feature parity with Node's crypto and b) increased your js bundle size considerably. FWIW webpack 5 also no longer defaults to using these questionable crypto polyfills anymore.

It is better to rely on JWT modules made to be consumed in browser environments. You can discover such modules on [jwt.io](https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript) under "JavaScript" libraries.

comments.author: garypotato
comments.body: I had the same issue that's because I am using Node.js v8, which doesn't include KeyObject in 'crypto' module. There are two ways to fix this issue: 1) update your node version to above v11; 2) don't use the latest version of jsonwebtoken.

title: Error: "alg" parameter "ES256" requires curve "prime256v1"
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether using the secp256k1 curve with ES256 makes tokens vulnerable, and the answer cites the IANA JOSE algorithms registry and RFC 8812 indicating the correct algorithm is ES256K and that ES256 requires the P‑256 curve.
security_topic: risk of using secp256k1 curve with ES256 JWT algorithm
question_text:
What I cannot find information about is what is the implication that I have used "wrong curve" when generating the keys?

In particular, I have used this command before: `openssl ecparam -name secp256k1 -genkey -noout -out key.pem`.
"Correct" command with the "correct" curve looks like this: `openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out key.pem`.

Are my tokens vulnerable to some attack or something, because I have used the "wrong curve" when generating the keys?
answer_text: No, it's just that the designated `alg` value for your key should be `ES256K` to be interoperable. The `ES256` algorithm requires the use of P-256 EC curve key.
thread_text:
ISSUE #862: Error: "alg" parameter "ES256" requires curve "prime256v1"
Author: kirillgroshkov
Date: 2022-12-21T19:18:33Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
Not a bug report, but a question.

My code started to fail with version 9 because of this error.
I've read the Changelog, Migration guide and source code that does this validation and see where it comes from.

I also can see that I can bypass this check with `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`.

What I cannot find information about is what is the implication that I have used "wrong curve" when generating the keys?

In particular, I have used this command before: `openssl ecparam -name secp256k1 -genkey -noout -out key.pem`.
"Correct" command with the "correct" curve looks like this: `openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out key.pem`.

Are my tokens vulnerable to some attack or something, because I have used the "wrong curve" when generating the keys?

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @panva 2022-12-22T12:12:19Z:
> Are my tokens vulnerable to some attack or something, because I have used the "wrong curve" when generating the keys?

No, it's just that the designated `alg` value for your key should be `ES256K` to be interoperable. The `ES256` algorithm requires the use of P-256 EC curve key.
---
[c2] @kirillgroshkov 2022-12-22T13:08:18Z:
> > Are my tokens vulnerable to some attack or something, because I have used the "wrong curve" when generating the keys?
> 
> No, it's just that the designated `alg` value for your key should be `ES256K` to be interoperable. The `ES256` algorithm requires the use of P-256 EC curve key.

Sorry, but what "interoperable" means?

Right now with the "wrong" key/curve I'm able to successfully verify my own issued keys. Same way, if someone else was using keys with "wrong curve" and share JWT with me - I will be able to successfully verify it (with the public key) (with `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes: true`).

What is it that is not "interoperable"?

I'm trying to assess the "severity" of this, is it like "recommendation" (that's fine to ignore), or "warning" (something might break, but what exactly?), or a hard security vulnerability (that my key may be brute-forced or something)?
---
[c3] @kirillgroshkov 2022-12-22T13:11:52Z:
Maybe interoperable means that if I issue a token using this "wrong" combination of `alg` and `key` - some other software might fail/refuse to verify my key? (without their own `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes`, which I don't control)

That sounds likely.

But then, if I control all "verifiers" of my JWT tokens - I should be "fine" by just doing `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes: true`?
---
[c4] @panva 2023-01-10T16:52:30Z:
> `ES256K` is not a valid algorithm for `jsonwebtoken`

`ES256K` absolutely IS a valid JWS algorithm. Registered in [IANA](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml) for use in JWS in [RFC 8812](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8812.html#name-jose-algorithms-registratio).

Edit: i see what you mean now, the algorithm isn't supported by **_this_** library. That is true. cc @jakelacey2012 this would very simple to add support for. Until then, [alternatives](https://jwt.io/libraries?language=Node.js) are available.
---
[c5] @jackson-dean 2023-07-12T17:02:25Z:
+1, would be nice to have support for this without needing to use the awkward `allowInvalidAsymmetricKeyTypes` flag.

title: Verification of RS256-encoded JWT does not work with Node 18
need_summary: The developer needed to know how to get RS256 JWT verification to work on Node 18, and the answer gave the concrete workaround of setting NODE_OPTIONS=--openssl-legacy-provider, citing a StackOverflow post and a Node.js issue as sources.
security_topic: RS256 JWT verification failure on Node 18 due to OpenSSL upgrade
question_text:
I'm trying to verify a JWT created by Keycloak. It uses the RS256 algorithm. That works with Node 16, but not with Node 18. I get the following error:
```
error:1E08010C:DECODER routines::unsupported
```
answer_text:
It seems like we need to add the following .env variable:
```
NODE_OPTIONS=--openssl-legacy-provider 
```
Reference: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/69962209/what-is-openssl-legacy-provider-in-node-js-v17
https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/40455

title: Does jsonwebtoken support use in browsers?
need_summary: The developer asked whether jsonwebtoken can be used in browsers to handle JWTs, and the maintainer replied that it is Node.js‑only and referenced the jwt.io libraries page (https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript).
security_topic: applicability of jsonwebtoken library to browser environments
question_text: I am wondering whether in turn this makes `jsonwebtoken` node.js specific and not suitable for use in a browser? If `jsonwebtoken` should work in a browser are there any specifics we should take into account? I am not seeing anything in the documentation.
answer_text: The `jsonwebtoken` library is only made for the Node.js runtime. For Browser or other Web-interoperable runtimes (e.g. Deno, Cloudlare Workers, ...) please see https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript.

title: Upgrading to react-scripts 5.0.0.0 causes major issues
need_summary: The developer needed to know that jsonwebtoken is not supported in browsers and the missing polyfills represent a security‑related limitation; the maintainer answered this, stating jsonwebtoken is Node‑only and linking to https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript as the source.
security_topic: incompatibility of Node‑only JWT library with browser after webpack upgrade
question_text: I was trying to upgrade my `react-scripts` to version `5.0.0` but when doing so I got a bunch of errors regarding `JWT` it says that it requires the following packages: 1: `crypto-browserify` 2. `crypto` 3. `stream` 4. `stream-browserify` and adding these packages with configuring webpack is just a pain and doesn't resolve the issue. and removing `JWT` completely gets rid of all of the errors
answer_text:
`jsonwebtoken` is a JWT implementation for Node.js. `jsonwebtoken` never officially catered to runtimes other than Node.js.

What you've been depending on up until now is webpack's automatic use of node module polyfills of questionable support, quality, security, and feature-parity with node's own modules. Those are not automatically applied in new versions of webpack, that is now used by the `create-react-app` resulting setup.

https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript lists a number of generic javascript jwt libraries that you could use for runtimes other than Node.js instead.

comments.author: panva
comments.body:
`jsonwebtoken` is a JWT implementation for Node.js. `jsonwebtoken` never officially catered to runtimes other than Node.js.

What you've been depending on up until now is webpack's automatic use of node module polyfills of questionable support, quality, security, and feature-parity with node's own modules. Those are not automatically applied in new versions of webpack, that is now used by the `create-react-app` resulting setup.

https://jwt.io/libraries?language=JavaScript lists a number of generic javascript jwt libraries that you could use for runtimes other than Node.js instead.

title: What is default behaviour if expiresIn option not set when signing?
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether a JWT signed without an expiresIn option ever expires, and the answer cites the JWT spec (RFC 7519) and jwt.io showing that no exp claim is added, so the token does not expire.
security_topic: default JWT expiration when exp claim omitted
question_text: So what's the default expiring date of the generated token? like after 24 hours, **or it never expires**?
answer_text: According to the spec (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7519#section-4.1.4), `exp` is an optional claim. So, if it's not defined, token is expired never.

title: can't import jsonwebtoken in modern typescript esm app
need_summary: How to correctly import the jsonwebtoken library in a modern TypeScript ESM project to access its sign/verify functions, answered by using the stipsan/jsonwebtoken-esm package (see https://github.com/stipsan/jsonwebtoken-esm).
security_topic: module import compatibility for jsonwebtoken in ESM TypeScript projects
question_text:
we can't properly import this library in a modern typescript project. here's the problem:
- `import * as jwt from "jsonwebtoken"`
    - export `default` contains what i need, sign, verify, etc
    - however, the types won't let me have it
- `@types/jsonwebtoken`
    - does not have any definition for a default export

as you can see there's an incompatibility between what can actually be imported at runtime, versus what the `@types` typings allow us to import. on one hand, this could be seen as a deficiency in the community `@types` typings

on the other hand, a fundamental fix for this problem would be:
- upgrade jsonwebtoken for first-class esm support
- maintain official typings

related issue #655

------

in the meantime, here's the hack i used to circumvent this problem

1. create a shim module `badmodules/jsonwebtoken.ts`
    ```typescript
    import * as _jsonwebtoken from "jsonwebtoken"
    const jsonwebtoken = <any>_jsonwebtoken

    import {
      sign as signType,
      verify as verifyType,
      SignOptions,
      VerifyOptions,
      Algorithm,
    } from "jsonwebtoken"

    const sign: typeof signType = jsonwebtoken.default.sign
    const verify: typeof verifyType = jsonwebtoken.default.verify

    export {
      sign,
      verify,
      Algorithm,
      SignOptions,
      VerifyOptions,
    }
    ```

2. import the shim module instead
    ```typescript
    import {sign, verify, SignOptions, VerifyOptions, Algorithm}
      from "./badmodules/jsonwebtoken.js"
    ```
answer_text: I was able to properly load jsonwebtoken with `import { default as jwt } from 'jsonwebtoken';` on ESNext

title: jsonwebtoken doesn't supported in webpack 5
need_summary: The developer needed to know if jsonwebtoken can be used in a browser build with webpack 5; the maintainer answered it cannot because it depends on Node's crypto module and pointed to the Web Cryptography API spec and the browser‑compatible jose library as concrete references.
security_topic: lack of browser support for jsonwebtoken and recommendation to use Web Crypto API based library
question_text: when building react with webpack5, I receive the error:
answer_text:
That's because `jsonwebtoken` is not built to be transpiled for the web browser runtime, under its hood it uses node's `crypto` module. We actually do not support browser environment as a runtime for this module.

We are not providing `jsonwebtoken` for the browser platform and would recommend use of JWT modules that utilize the browser built-in Web Cryptography API instead, e.g. `jose`.

title: Decimal timestamps cause JsonWebTokenError on signature verification
need_summary: The developer asked if the JWT library should handle decimal timestamps or if the token encoding is incorrect, and the maintainer answered that the JWT spec (IANA registered claims) requires these claims to be JSON numbers, not strings.
security_topic: JWT numeric claim type enforcement
question_text: Thanks for the quick reply @panva . So, you're saying that - rather than this package doing something like `parseFloat` to catch this - the encoding process is at fault here, correct?
answer_text: Yes. Whomever produces that JWT produces it incorrectly. It's meant to be a JSON number type rather than a string.
thread_text:
ISSUE #764: Decimal timestamps cause JsonWebTokenError on signature verification
Author: tklie
Date: 2021-02-15T12:30:07Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Description

The token verification fails, even though the token is a valid JWT.

### Reproduction

To reproduce, provide any token with decimal timestamps. This will be decoded to something like:

```json
{
    "aud": "14",
    "jti": "e1fd9735bb925432588c61bfac9ad1edd7237d11dbc008506f29329bf7260ff48106142ac09227a5",
    "iat": "1613388071.325008",
    "nbf": "1613388071.325013",
    "exp": "1644924071.299660",
    "sub": "5",
    "scopes": []
}
```

Trying to verify this same token's signature against the public key causes following error:

```
JsonWebTokenError {
    name: 'JsonWebTokenError',
    message: 'invalid nbf value'
}
```

After some initial debugging, this error seems to be caused by this package type-checking the `iat`, `nbf` and `exp` fields for being of type `number`, but the decoding process returning decimal timestamps as `string`.

### Environment

- **Version of this library used:** 8.5.1
- **Version of the platform or framework used, if applicable:** Ubuntu 20.04
- **Other relevant versions (language, server software, OS, browser):** Node 12.19.0
- **Other modules/plugins/libraries that might be involved:** Token issued by Laravel package Passport


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @panva 2021-02-15T12:57:44Z:
Hello @TKlie the type check for a number is correct.

```js
> JSON.stringify({ iat: 127.32 })
'{"iat":127.32}'
> JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ iat: 127.32 }))
{ iat: 127.32 }
```

These are IANA registered claims with a type defined by the specification.

title: error:04075070:rsa routines:RSA_sign:digest too big for rsa key
need_summary: The developer needed to know why RSA signing fails with 'digest too big' and that the RSA key must be at least 2048 bits per the JWA specification, as explained in the maintainer’s comment referencing the JWA spec.
security_topic: RSA key size requirement for JWT signing algorithms
question_text:
Hmmm so I can make sure I understand (as I don't know anything about cryptography), what is the relation (if any) between the algorithm (RS512, RS256) I would choose and the modulus length ?

I can sign my token with, say, the RS256 algorithm and a modulus of 2048, if I wanted ? That is, they don't need to match
answer_text: modulus is one of the components of your RSA private key, its length must be 2048 bits to be universally usable with JOSE. Your key's bit length is 512, generate a key of size 2048 and you'll be able to use all RSA based signing algorithms (it doesn't matter what the algorithm's "number" is since that only dictates the hash algorithm).

title: Caching Public Keys?
need_summary: The developer asked whether a JWT public key can be cached for repeated verify calls, and the answer cites Node.js’s `createPublicKey` (available in Node v11.6.0+) as the concrete way to obtain a reusable KeyObject.
security_topic: caching public key for JWT verification
question_text: What I'm wondering is if there is a way I can "cache" the public key after it's decrypted so that on subsequent calls to `verify`, it doesn't have to continuously redo the work of decoding that key.
thread_text:
ISSUE #734: Caching Public Keys?
Author: jasonterando
Date: 2020-07-28T23:03:45Z
Labels: 
State: open

[c0]
### Describe the problem you'd like to have solved

I'm writing a micro-service in which I'm trying to squeeze every bit of performance that I can.  I am using `verify` to validate a JWT token against a public key file that I've read in as a string (`-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----` etc.) .  It work fine.

What I'm wondering is if there is a way I can "cache" the public key after it's decrypted so that on subsequent calls to `verify`, it doesn't have to continuously redo the work of decoding that key.  I checked the results coming back from `verify` when setting the option `complete` to true, but didn't see anything along these lines.

### Describe the ideal solution

In the results that come back from `verify`, include a property of the decoded key that I can pass back in on subsequent calls to `verify`.

## Alternatives and current work-arounds

n/a - as mentioned, passing in the entire PEM string to `verify` each time works


--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @luneo7 2020-08-18T20:59:11Z:
You can actually do like this if you are using NodeJS >= v11.6.0:
```
import {createPublicKey, KeyObject} from 'crypto';

function parsePublicKey(pKey: string): KeyObject {
  return createPublicKey({
    key: pKey,
    format: 'pem',
  });
}
```
With that `KeyObject` you can call `verify` as much as you want

title: Uncaught ReferenceError: global is not defined
need_summary: The developer asked if jsonwebtoken can be used in the browser and the maintainer answered that it is not supported and recommended using browser‑based JWT modules that rely on the Web Cryptography API (see the Web Crypto API specification).
security_topic: browser incompatibility of jsonwebtoken
question_text:
I am trying to use jsonwebtoken in angular with socketio 
`const token = jwt.sign({ foo: "bar" }, "shhhhh");`

but it gives the following error:

We are not providing `jsonwebtoken` for the browser platform and would recommend use of JWT modules that utilize the browser built-in [`Web Cryptography API`](https://www.w3.org/TR/WebCryptoAPI/) instead.

FYI, we also do not have a single occurance of node's `global` variable in our code either.

title: Use a default of `["HS256"]` for `verify` to be in sync with default for `sign`
need_summary: The developer asked if jwt.verify accepts all algorithms (including "none") by default, and the answer cites the verify.js source at v8.5.1 (https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/v8.5.1/verify.js#L99-L118) showing it does not.
security_topic: default algorithm handling in JWT verification
question_text: By default `sign` uses `options.algorithm: "HS256"`. In contrast `verify` does not use `options.algorithms: ["HS256"]` by default - but instead accepts all algorithms. This means by default we sign with HS256 but we verify and accept all algorithms - for example also the `none` algorithm. If we're setting a default in sign we should set the same default in verify - and keep them in sync. Thoughts?
answer_text: Verify's `algorithm` option default value is derived from the `secretOrPublicKey` argument value and it never defaults to accepting **all algorithms**. The accidental acceptance of `none` tokens is **also prevented**.
thread_text:
ISSUE #728: Use a default of `["HS256"]` for `verify` to be in sync with default for `sign`
Author: daniel-j-h
Date: 2020-06-29T12:49:41Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
By default `sign` uses `options.algorithm: "HS256"`.

In contrast `verify` does not use `options.algorithms: ["HS256"]` by default - but instead accepts all algorithms.

This means by default we sign with HS256 but we verify and accept all algorithms - for example also the `none` algorithm.

If we're setting a default in sign we should set the same default in verify - and keep them in sync.

Thoughts?

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @panva 2020-06-29T12:55:42Z:
source: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/v8.5.1/verify.js#L99-L118

> but instead accepts all algorithms

That is a false statement.

Verify's `algorithm` option default value is derived from the `secretOrPublicKey` argument value and it never defaults to accepting **all algorithms**. The accidental acceptance of `none` tokens is **also prevented**.

What lead you this expectation of accepting everything?
---
[c2] @daniel-j-h 2020-06-29T13:30:45Z:
Here is an example of what I mean. Create a token with algorithm none

```js
> jwt.sign({ user: 42 }, undefined, { algorithm: 'none' });
'eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.'
```

The key is not needed - I set it to undefined.

By default now we can verify that token without having to explicitly allow none as an algorithm

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.')
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

and also works in this scenario when we accidentally pass undefined (or anything else false-y as an argument)

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.', process.env.MYKEY) // oops env var undefined
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

It would be best if we could make this explicit - the user should pass `algorithms: ["none"]` if the user really knows what this means and implies.

This is the case for all algorithm options. By default sign sets `HS256` as an algorithm but in verify by default we accept all algorithms e.g. we also accept a token signed with `HS512`.
---
[c3] @panva 2020-06-29T13:38:06Z:
> but instead accepts all algorithms

so, this is not true.

For the `none` being explicitly required as algorithms option we already have #711 as duplicate.

For the rest, accepting HS512 when you, by default, sign with HS256 isn't that big of a deal. However, we think that in general defaulting to use HS256 even when a private key value is passed in is a problem in itself and will be changing that for next major too, so that the algorithm is derived of the `secretOrPrivateKey` argument same as for verify today.
---

title: Error while providing algorith option to jwt.sign()

security_topic: invalid RSA private key for JWT RS384 signing
question_text: The library produces error when an algorithm option is passed to jwt.sign() method.

Author: pavittarx

title: Less Secure (jwt token decodes without any secret)
need_summary: The developer asked whether a JWT signed with a secret is secure, and the answer cites the JWT specification (RFC 7519) and Auth0 documentation explaining that JWTs are only signed (not encrypted) and can be decoded without a secret.
security_topic: JWT signing vs encryption and security of token-based authentication
question_text: I just wanted to know is this secure to do token-based authentication in a web app.
answer_text:
`jwt.sign` is for signing a token, not encrypting it. With signing, you use a private key to sign a message so that a consumer of the message can use a public key (or the private key, depending if you chose a symmetric algorithm to sign the payload) to verify its authenticity.

For more information; check out this document (https://auth0.com/docs/tokens/references/jwt-structure). Also, this RFC (https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519) specifies the JSON web token standard, as well as what some JWT claims are used for.

Hope this helps!

ISSUE #706: Less Secure (jwt token decodes without any secret)
Author: ssatyamchauhan

Labels:

Team JWT,  I have created a token using jwt.sign where I have passed my own secret and then I copied the token pasted it on jwt.io website and I was amazed it decodes my token without any secret 
 and showing usernames and passwords.

Here Is the toke for Demo purpose: ```eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2Vybm1hZSI6InNzYXR5YW1jaGF1aGFuIiwicGFzc3dvcmQiOiJ3aHlpdGlzbWUiLCJpYXQiOjE1ODUxMzM0ODMsImV4cCI6MTU4NTM5MjY4M30.bKtmn03-ZnAAzNxnNk9ZPlrsbbk8lUThMt24gwL-r2w```
I just wanted to know is this secure to do token-based authentication in a web app.
#### Hoping for the quick response.

[c1] @yacineMTB 2020-03-25T14:22:01Z:
`jwt.sign` is for signing a token, not encrypting it. With signing, you use a private key to sign a message so that a consumer of the message can use a public key (or the private key, depending if you chose a symmetric algorithm to sign the payload) to verify its authenticity.

For more information; check out [this document](https://auth0.com/docs/tokens/references/jwt-structure). 
Also, [this RFC](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519) specifies the JSON web token standard, as well as what some JWT claims are used for.

Hope this helps!

[c2] @jhiner 2020-03-25T14:43:15Z:
To add to @yacineMTB 's response, you can decode a token without verifying its signature. This is why you see this behavior with jwt.io. This distinction is referenced in the readme here: https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken#jwtdecodetoken--options

[c3] @panva 2020-03-25T14:59:25Z:
@ssatyamchauhan to sign its payload. So that when you receive the token you can verify it was not tampered with. This uses JWS (JSON Web Signatures) to provide integrity protection, NOT CONFIDENTIALITY.

For confidentiality various JWE (JSON Web Encryption) schemes are available, not in this package tho.

Also, in jwt.io, if you provide your secret under the `VERIFY SIGNATURE` section, you will see `Signature Verified`. Without that, you will see `Invalid Signature`.

[c6] @panva 2020-03-25T15:09:21Z:
`jsonwebtoken` does not provide encryption, only signatures.

https://github.com/panva/jose can be used for both signing and encryption, but please consider reading up on the topic and specifications first before jumping in and choosing a cipher suite poorly for your use case.

title: TypeError: e is not an object or null
need_summary: The developer asked if jsonwebtoken can be used in the browser to sign JWTs, and the maintainer clarified that it is not supported for browser runtimes and advised using JWT libraries that use the Web Cryptography API (see the Web Crypto API specification).
security_topic: unsupported use of jsonwebtoken in browser environment
question_text: I was embedding metabase dashboard in my angular app thus I needed to use jsonwebtoken. I have used jwt.sign method to encrypt my data in token. By starting project on localhost with 'ng serve' everything works fine, but if I will build project I keep getting an error in console **TypeError: e is not an object or null**
answer_text:
That's because `jsonwebtoken` is not built to be transpiled, under its hood it uses node's `crypto` module that your webpack bundle has a registered polyfill for. We can't control that, **nor do we actually support browser environment as a runtime for this module**.

We are not providing `jsonwebtoken` for the browser platform and would recommend use of JWT modules that utilize the browser built-in [`Web Cryptography API`](https://www.w3.org/TR/WebCryptoAPI/) instead.

title: How do we set a refresh token and set expiry time for a jwt?
need_summary: The developer asked how to add an expiry time and refresh token for JWTs, and the maintainer answered that the expiry can be set via the `expiresIn` option in jsonwebtoken’s `sign` function (see the library README) and that refresh‑token logic must be implemented by the user with guidance from the node‑jsonwebtoken refreshing JWTs documentation.
security_topic: JWT expiration and refresh token implementation
question_text: I am following an article and want to implement JWT on a reactjs app with a fake backend and I am following this article https://jasonwatmore.com/post/2017/12/07/react-redux-jwt-authentication-tutorial-example So far, I have added the login and logout with but I don't know how to add an expiry time for jwt and how to add refresh token for jwt.
answer_text:
You can add it using the expiresIn option on the sign function. You can read more about the function signature [here](https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken/blob/master/README.md#jwtsignpayload-secretorprivatekey-options-callback).

how to add refresh token for jwt

This library doesn't have logic for refreshing tokens. You'll have to add the logic yourself. [You can find some additional information/hints here](https://github.com/auth0/node-jsonwebtoken#refreshing-jwts).

title: what is the metric for expiresIn attribute in the JWT token ?
need_summary: The developer needed to know whether the JWT expiresIn attribute is interpreted in seconds or milliseconds and how to correctly compare the token's exp claim with JavaScript timestamps; the answer cites the jsonwebtoken library version ^9.0.2 and explains that numeric values are seconds while string values are milliseconds.
security_topic: units of expiresIn attribute in JWT token
question_text: Should i assign the `value` for `expiresIn` attribute in seconds or milliseconds?
answer_text:
If it's a numerical value, it will be interpreted as seconds.

if `expiresIn` is 1, as in `typeof 1` returns `'number'`; it will be interpreted as expiring in 1 second.

If it is a string value, it will be interpreted as milliseconds. If expiresIn is `"100"`, it will be interpreted as expiring in 100 milliseconds.

Hope that helps!

title: Add option to ignore signature validation (e. g. for dev/test purposes)
need_summary: The developer wanted to know if they could safely ignore JWT signature verification for testing, and the maintainer answered concretely by linking to the verify.js source at commit a6235fa561b5c30884c97ea0b30c3db3b546ae2c where the option could be added.
security_topic: ignoring JWT signature verification for testing
question_text: Add option to ignore signature validation (e. g. for dev/test purposes)
answer_text:
I think it is too risky to add that option to the `verify()` function, without signature the rest of checks do not make sense, you can not trust the information you got. Also I think they key point is here:
> for a special edge situation

I'd say to try to solve that special edge case by fixing the interoperability between both.

Other possible workarounds:
* You could mock the Token Provider depending on your tests.
* You can build an abstraction using `.decode()` as you said in testing, really... any other check without signature verification can be forced to fail whenever you want.
  * Even that abstraction could do `decode()` + `sign()` another token with same payload and `none` algorithm or use one secret for testing an use one of `HS` algorithms + `verify()`.

Anyway whatever you do it has the risk to end up running in production due to a misconfiguration. 😅 

PS: Nice way to present your request 👏

ISSUE #665: Add option to ignore signature validation (e. g. for dev/test purposes)
Author: rockebee
Date: 2020-01-20T14:51:59Z
Labels: 
State: closed

[c0]
### Describe the problem you'd like to have solved

> In dev and test environments it may be feasible to work with a test JWT token which has no valid signature, e. g. for cases where the token provider can not be modified to create tokens in a manner how a relying party needs it for a special edge situation. In this case the JWT payload could be modified manually be the developer to match/test the requirement, but the current jsonwebtoken implementation does not allow to use this invalid token within ```jwt.verify()``` function.

### Describe the ideal solution

> Adding a new option ```ignoreSignature``` to the existing set of options (like ```ignoreExpiration``` and ```ignoreNotBefore```) would allow developers to use self-modified tokens for tests but still having checks for proper ```issuer```, ```subject```, ```audience``` in place.

## Alternatives and current work-arounds

> Using of ```jwt.decode()``` instead of ```jwt.verify()``` helps in at least getting the JWT decoded properly, but as mentioned above does not allow for getting other verification checks run (```issuer``` etc.)

### Additional context

> no additional input here
